newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress Party re-elects president Kesri.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress Party re-elects president Kesri.

text.p: The president of the Indian Congress Party, Sitaram Kesri, was re-elected on Thursday in a rare internal ballot and said his victory vindicated a controversial decision that sparked a political crisis.

"This election justifies my decision to withdraw support to (former prime minister H.D.) Deve Gowda's government, which was hurting the prestige of the country and the Congress party," a delighted Kesri told reporters.

He was referring to Congress's shock decision in March to withdraw parliamentary support to the 10-month-old United Front government. The move plunged the country into political turmoil, triggered a confidence vote in which Deve Gowda was toppled and drew sharp criticism from Kesri's opponents.
Congress renewed its crucial backing of the 15-party coalition in parliament only after agreeing to replace Deve Gowda with Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral.
Chief polling officer Oscar Fernandes said Kesri won 6,224 of the 7,557 votes polled. Maharashtra strongman Sharad Pawar got 882 votes, Rajesh Pilot had 354 votes and 97 were invalid.
Kesri said he would strive to fulfill the hopes and aspirations of Congress supporters who had kept faith with him and presented him with a thumping victory.
Jubiliant Kesri supporters danced and shouted slogans outside Congress headquarters in central Delhi, exploding fire crackers and waving saffron, green and white Congress flags.
It was only the third election in the 112-year history of India's oldest political party, traditionally dominated by charismatic leaders.

Once the driving force behind the movement against colonial rule, Congress has ruled India for all but five years since independence in 1947, with former prime ministers Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi in power for 37 years.
Kesri, 76, swept aside the challenges from two younger party leaders who stood on a platform of rejuvenating an ailing party that suffered a crushing defeat in general elections last year.
Both his rivals, Pawar and Pilot, conceded defeat and pledged to work with Kesri to strengthen the party. "We will work together. This is the Congress culture," Pawar told reporters.
Asked if Kesri's victory would jeopardise his own position as leader of the Congress party in parliament, Pawar said: "Mr Kesri is the appointing authority and I will accept his decision."
Pilot told reporters: "I will work with Mr Kesri while continuing our struggle for the party's principles."

Kesri's victory will end bitter bickering that had marked the internal polls, Congress official Jagdish Tytler told Reuters. "Kesri will now legitimately have the support of younger people and will be a guiding force," Tytler said.

Congress received another shot in the arm when a Delhi court dropped charges against four former Congress ministers in connection with a money-laundering scandal which forced the resignations of seven ministers last year.
Party officials say a decision by Rajiv Gandhi's Italian-born widow, Sonia, to join Congress could also revive the party's flagging fortunes.
